planting.note: Plant small divisions or rooted sprigs in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; dwarf pennywort roots readily at every leaf node and spreads quickly in warm, damp conditions, so a small planting fills in fast.

directions: Plant small rooted sprigs into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; dwarf pennywort is a very low, fast-spreading creeper with tiny, round, scalloped, bright-green leaves on thread-like stems that root at each node as they travel, quickly knitting into a lush green carpet in damp, shaded ground. It is useful as a soft filler around container edges, along shaded shady bed margins that stay damp, or at the moist border of a water feature, and is also grown submersed or emersed in aquariums and paludariums as an easy, fast-growing accent plant. It spreads aggressively wherever moisture and shade both stay high, so give it a contained spot or a location where its spread is wanted rather than a tidy formal bed; it is far less vigorous, and can struggle, in drier or sunnier conditions. In frost-free to nearly frost-free climates it stays evergreen; farther north within its range it dies back in winter and returns from the roots in spring.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in humus-rich, moist but well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; February daphne resents root disturbance and transplants poorly once established, so choose its permanent site carefully from the start.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in partial shade and leave it undisturbed once sited, since daphnes resent root disturbance; February daphne is a small deciduous shrub cherished for its very early, intensely fragrant, rosy-purple to pink flowers that wreathe the bare stems in late winter, often opening while snow is still on the ground and well before almost anything else in the garden. Flowers give way to bright red berries in summer, and the plant is compact and upright, fitting neatly into a shaded shrub border or entry planting where the winter fragrance can be enjoyed at close range. It performs best in cooler summer climates with a real winter chill and can be short-lived or stressed in prolonged summer heat and humidity. Every part of the plant, especially the berries and sap, is toxic if ingested and the sap can irritate skin, so site it away from children and pets who might be tempted by the colorful fruit, and wear gloves when pruning. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and avoid disturbing the root zone once planted.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in well-drained soil, including dry, chalky, or alkaline ground, in partial to full shade; spurge laurel resents root disturbance and transplants poorly once established, so choose its permanent site carefully from the start.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil, tolerant of poor, dry, chalky, or alkaline ground, in partial to full shade beneath established trees; spurge laurel is a low, rounded evergreen shrub notable for tolerating deep, dry shade better than almost any other flowering shrub, with glossy, leathery, dark-green leaves clustered near the branch tips and small, fragrant, yellow-green flowers tucked among the upper leaves in late winter, followed by black berries in summer. It asks for very little once established — no supplemental water in most climates and no feeding — making it a useful, low-maintenance evergreen for the difficult dry shade under mature trees where few flowering shrubs will grow at all. Every part of the plant, especially the berries and sap, is toxic if ingested, and the sap can cause skin irritation or blistering on contact, so wear gloves when pruning and site it away from children and pets. In parts of its introduced range, notably the Pacific Northwest, it has become locally invasive by self-seeding into woodland understories, so check local guidance before planting it and remove any unwanted seedlings promptly.
sources: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board

planting.note: Plant container or balled shrubs in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil, including chalky or alkaline ground, in full sun to partial shade; wayfaring tree is exceptionally tough and adaptable, tolerating drought, wind, and difficult soil once established.

directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil, including dry, chalky, or alkaline ground, in full sun to partial shade; wayfaring tree is a large, rugged, deciduous viburnum long used for hedging and windbreaks across Europe, with felted, gray-green, textured leaves and flat clusters of creamy-white flowers in late spring that develop into berries passing through red on their way to a final glossy black, so a single cluster often shows both colors together in late summer — a striking two-tone effect that also feeds birds. Fall color runs from yellow to deep red-purple. It is one of the toughest large viburnums available, shrugging off poor soil, wind, drought, and neglect once established, and works well as an informal hedge, screen, or woodland-margin shrub where a tidier plant would struggle. Prune right after flowering if shaping is needed; otherwise it needs very little routine care. The felted leaves and stems are a useful identification feature that distinguishes it from smoother-leaved viburnums.

planting.note: Plant container or balled shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Siebold's viburnum tolerates the light shade of a woodland margin better than many large flowering shrubs and grows into a substantial small tree over time.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Siebold's viburnum is a large, handsome, tree-like viburnum from Japan with bold, deep-green, leathery leaves and, in late spring, dense, rounded clusters of creamy-white flowers with a distinctive, somewhat pungent fragrance that carries on the air. The real show follows in late summer as the fruit clusters ripen through a striking sequence from green to pink to bright red and finally glossy black, all held on showy, persistent, contrasting red stalks (pedicels) that remain colorful even after the birds strip the berries. Give it room to grow, since with age it develops into a substantial small tree well suited to the back of a shrub border, a woodland margin, or as a specimen with high, filtered shade from taller trees overhead. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood; the naturally handsome, layered branching habit needs little shaping. A tough, long-lived, four-season shrub for a partly shaded spot with room to spare.
